```text
                                                       Near-Exact Computation of Independent Chip Model
                                                        Placement Probabilities for Thousands of Players
                                                                                         Wataru Inariba∗

                                                                                           GTO Wizard




arXiv:2610.06028v1 [cs.DS] 5 Oct 2026
                                                                                           October 2026



                                                                                              Abstract
                                                      The Independent Chip Model (ICM) converts the chip stacks of the players remaining in
                                                  a poker tournament into finishing-place probabilities and prize equities. It is the standard
                                                  model in tournament solvers, but its definition considers all possible finishing orders, and exact
                                                  computation has been regarded as intractable for large fields. The same mathematics appears in
                                                  other fields; for instance, the ICM is a Plackett–Luce ranking model with stacks as weights. We
                                                  present DE-ICM, a deterministic algorithm that computes the placement probabilities of all n
                                                  players for all paid places in O(M n2 ) time, where the number M of quadrature nodes is fixed for
                                                  the admissible inputs and the target accuracy. Its numerical scheme allows the target to be set
                                                  close to the accuracy of double-precision arithmetic. The algorithm evaluates a classical integral
                                                  representation in which, conditional on a player’s exponential clock, the number of players ahead
                                                  is Poisson-binomial. A double-exponential quadrature on a single grid evaluates every integral;
                                                  its truncation errors have closed-form bounds, and the step size, which controls the discretization
                                                  error, follows from the field size. A numerically stable deconvolution then recovers each player’s
                                                  leave-one-out coefficients in O(n) time from one shared product. On exactly solvable instances
                                                  with up to 4,000 players, the worst observed relative error of an equity is 4.0 × 10−14 and the
                                                  worst absolute error of a placement probability 1.1 × 10−14 . The full placement matrix for 1,000
                                                  players takes 0.2 seconds on one CPU core.


                                        1        Introduction
                                        In a poker tournament, chips are not money. Prizes are paid by finishing position, so the value of a
                                        stack depends on the stacks of every remaining player and on the prize structure. The Independent
                                        Chip Model (ICM) is the standard way to convert stacks into value: it defines a distribution
                                        over finishing orders by repeatedly drawing the next finisher with probability proportional to the
                                        remaining stacks [11, 22]. In a tournament solver that approximates equilibrium strategies [34], the
                                        equities under the ICM serve as the payoffs at the end of a hand, either directly or as the initial
                                        values of an iteration that refines them [10].
                                            The defining recursion enumerates all finishing orders. For n players, direct enumeration costs
                                        O(n!) time, and dynamic programming over subsets of players costs O(n2n ) time and O(2n ) space;
                                        neither is practical beyond about 30 players. Larger fields have relied on Monte Carlo simulation
                                        of finishing orders [29] or on other approximation methods, such as the undisclosed method used
```

```text
by HoldemResources [14]. Since a tournament solver may require thousands of ICM evaluations,
and small differences in equity can affect the resulting strategies, we aim for fast, deterministic
evaluation whose accuracy can be tuned through an explicit error budget.
    This paper describes DE-ICM (Algorithm 1), which computes the matrix of placement probabil-
ities Qi,r for every player i and every paid place r ≤ m, with accuracy that can approach that of
double-precision arithmetic. It runs in O(M n2 ) time, where the number M of quadrature nodes
is derived once from the field size, stack-ratio bound and target accuracy, and is shared across
admissible instances. The matrix rather than the equities is the natural output because the equity
under any prize structure is a linear functional of it. Its entries and partial sums, such as the
probability of finishing in the money, are also of interest in themselves.
    The starting point is a classical integral representation (Theorem 2.2). The ICM is a Plackett–
Luce model [21, 28] with the stacks as weights, and in the exponential-race representation of that
model, players are ordered by increasing values of independent exponential clocks with rates given
by the stacks. Given one player’s clock value, each other player independently finishes ahead or
behind, so the number ahead has a Poisson-binomial distribution. Integrating these conditional
probabilities against the exponential density of that player’s clock gives the placement probabilities.
This representation arises in the analysis of the move-to-front rule for self-organizing lists [8, 9] and
was recently rediscovered for propensity estimation in learning to rank [18].

Quadrature. General-purpose quadrature typically adapts its quadrature nodes to the relevant
ranges of clock values, which vary with the input stack distribution. In contrast, we normalize the
stacks and evaluate all integrals on a fixed grid using a double-exponential (DE) transformation
followed by the trapezoidal rule. We assume throughout that the largest and the smallest stack
differ by at most a factor of ρ = 109 , a conservative bound for the tournament settings of interest.
The truncation errors have closed-form bounds, and the step h follows from a prediction of the
discretization error that is checked against measurements (Section 3).

Leave-one-out. The Poisson-binomial generating function for each player excludes the player’s
own factor. At each quadrature node, recomputing the product separately for every player costs
O(n2 m). Dividing the full product by each player’s linear factor costs O(n) per player, or O(n2 )
in total, but previous work avoided this approach because of numerical instability [18]. Here the
division is stable once its direction is chosen by comparing the player’s conditional probability to a
threshold, and its error satisfies an absolute bound. Within that bound, rounding can still leave a
residual that turns into an appreciable relative error after quadrature, so we remove it by clamping
each step to the bounds that the exact recurrence satisfies (Section 4).

Production use. An earlier version of the method, with the same integral representation and
quadrature on a fixed grid based on the exp-sinh transformation, has been in production use at GTO
Wizard since 2024, inside a tournament solver for fields of up to 4,096 players. The direction-switched
leave-one-out deconvolution has been in use since then in an ICM calculator that returns the equities
of all players. A GTO Wizard blog post [2] reported the existence and accuracy of this earlier version
without describing the method. This paper adds an explicit error budget and parameter selection
for a double-exponential rule suited to exponentially decaying integrands (Section 3), a stability
analysis and a clamp for the leave-one-out recurrence (Section 4), and a validation suite at the level
of double-precision arithmetic (Section 5), along with comparisons with marginalized Plackett–Luce
[18] and Log-Age Quadrature ICM [32] (Section 6.3). The parameters and the experiments reported
here were developed for this paper and are independent of the product.
```

```text
Recent related work. Two recent works, MPL [18] and LAQI [32], arrive at the same integral
representation and present numerical frameworks for evaluating it. They show that Plackett–Luce
propensities and ICM equities, respectively, can be computed deterministically for large fields, with
much higher accuracy than sampling. LAQI cites the above GTO Wizard blog post as its starting
point. DE-ICM differs in deriving its grid from an error budget rather than from the instance, in
computing the placement matrix at O(n2 ) operations per node, and in its validation against exact
references for up to 4,000 players (Table 6 in Section 6.3).

    Section 5 validates the algorithm against families of exactly solvable instances that scale to 4,000
players and reports runtimes. Section 6 relates the method to earlier work, and Section 7 concludes
the paper.

2.1   The Independent Chip Model
A field of n players has stacks s1 , . . . , sn > 0 with total S = i si . Prizes π1 ≥ π2 ≥ · · · ≥ πm > 0

That is, the winner is drawn with probability proportional to stack, then the runner-up is drawn
among the remaining players with probability proportional to stack, and so on. This is the Plackett–
Luce distribution [21, 28] with weights si . Two quantities are of interest: the placement probabilities
Qi,r = P(σr = i), which form a doubly stochastic n × n matrix, and the equities Vi = m

Because Equation (1) is invariant under si 7→ λ si for λ > 0, only the ratios of stacks matter; we use
this freedom in Section 3.1. Table 1 collects the notation.

2.2   The exponential race
Lemma 2.1 (Exponential race). Let T1 , . . . , Tn be independent with Tj ∼ Exp(sj ), and let σ order
the players by increasing clock, so that σ1 has the smallest clock. Then σ has the ICM distribution
given by Equation (1).

Proof. The minimum of independent exponentials is attained by player i with probability si /S.
Conditional on player i having the minimum at time t, the residual times Tj − t, j ̸= i, are again
independent exponentials with rates sj by the memoryless property. Induction over the remaining
players gives Equation (1).

    The lemma gives a simple way to sample an ICM finishing order: draw the clocks and sort them
[29]. It also corresponds to the Gumbel construction of the Plackett–Luce distribution [19, 33], since
− log Tj is a Gumbel variable with location log sj , and to the continuous-time description of the
move-to-front rule (Section 6.1).

2.3   Integral representation of placement probabilities
Fix a player i and condition on Ti = t. Player j ̸= i finishes ahead of i exactly when Tj < t, an event
of probability 1 − qj (t) with qj (t) = e−sj t , and these events are independent across j. The number of
```

```text
Compression and headroom. Near the junction of the two branches the lattice is compressed:
its local spacing in log t is h d log t/dx = h (1 + e−x ), a factor 1.57 where t = 1 (x ≈ 0.57) and 1.05

by that factor and would need a correspondingly finer step. The headroom of Equation (5) moves

every other transition lies further to the right, on the logarithmic branch. What remains on the
compressed branch are the integrands for the early places, whose bumps are broad (Figure 1). The
price of headroom is window length, one unit for each factor e, and the choice of c balances two
costs. The narrowest bumps lie at t ≈ b∗ c (Lemma 3.2), where b∗ ≈ 1.6 and the compression is
about 1 + 1/(b∗ c). The number of nodes grows with this factor, through the step, and with the
window length W ≈ 31; their product is smallest at b∗ c ≈ W , that is, at c ≈ 20. We take this value
for all results of the paper.

The exp-sinh rule. The other double-exponential transformation for [0, ∞), t = exp( π2 sinh x),

3.3    Error budget
The error of a computed placement probability has three sources: the truncation of the integral to a
finite window (Proposition 3.1), the discretization of the integral by the trapezoidal rule (Lemma 3.2
and Equation (11)), and rounding in floating-point arithmetic (Remark 3.3).
```

```text
Remark 3.3 (Rounding). The coefficients at each node are products and sums of non-negative
numbers, and Section 4 delivers them with an absolute error of O(nu); the quadrature sum√ over M
positive weights adds O(M u). The resulting floor is O((n+M )u) in the worst case and O( n + M u)
typically, about 10−14 for n ≈ M ≈ 103 . This accounting is heuristic, and we treat the floor as an
estimate to be confirmed by measurement (Section 5.1).


4     All players at once: stable leave-one-out deconvolution
                                                                                      \i
At a fixed node t, the integrals of Equation (3) need the leave-one-out coefficient Cr (t) of Equation (2)
for every player i and every place index r < m. This section obtains all of them from one product
in O(n2 ) operations, with a stability guarantee. Throughout, t is fixed and suppressed, qj = e−s̃j t is
the probability that player j finishes behind the conditioned player, and the stacks are normalized
and sorted so that s̃1 ≤ · · · ≤ s̃n , hence q1 ≥ · · · ≥ qn .
```
